summary: The article reviews progress and remaining gaps in ADA-compliant public transportation since the Americans with Disabilities Act passed on July 26, 1990. It covers persistent problems such as funding shortfalls and broken accessibility equipment, rider feedback, and new efforts including a real-time accessibility app, agency-advocacy partnerships, and increased DOT audits. It concludes that the work toward fully inclusive transit is ongoing.
one_line: An overview of ADA transit accessibility progress since 1990, covering ongoing challenges, rider feedback, smart technology, partnerships, and DOT audits through 2024.
key_facts: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was passed on July 26, 1990, mandating removal of barriers in public life including transportation.
Wheelchair ramps, elevator access to subway platforms, and audio-visual announcements in stations and vehicles are cited as direct results of ADA compliance efforts.
On November 15, 2023, the National Council on Disability released a report showing that not all transit systems are fully ADA compliant.
Lack of funding, especially in rural and underserved areas, continues to hinder accessibility enhancements.
On December 5, 2023, accessibility consultant James Marshall said innovation in public transportation must not 'leave people with disabilities behind.'
On January 10, 2024, wheelchair user Jessica Rodriguez said accessibility is 'a hit or miss' and that she has been stranded because of a broken lift or an unexpected step at a boarding area.
The Metropolitan Transportation Network (MTN) has begun holding monthly forums where riders with disabilities can give real-time feedback on accessibility issues.
On February 21, 2024, the City Transit Authority announced a mobile app giving real-time updates on the status of accessible features, such as elevator outages and temporarily non-compliant routes.
The City Transit Authority's app was conceived by a task force of developers with disabilities.
On March 5, 2024, MTN and Accessibility for All (AFA) announced a collaboration to review and revise transportation policies and provide hands-on staff training led by trainers with disabilities.
The Department of Transportation (DOT) has increased the frequency of accessibility audits; the latest round concluded on April 17, 2024 with recommended improvements and allocated federal funds.
Systematic reforms include accessibility committees within transit agencies, regular maintenance checks for accessibility equipment, and using ADA compliance as a key performance indicator.
